instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# ARC demo grounding

Use with an ARC-solving skill when a puzzle offers costly demonstrations and submissions.

## task-55b70234 recurrence: fill framed interiors and 3x3 centers (expanded validation)

This task family uses shape-specific interior recoloring. Do not apply one fill color indiscriminately to every hollow outline: identify frame geometry and the corresponding center/interior color from demos.

A prior solved instance (background 8) demonstrated hollow 5x5 frames with 3x3 interiors filled 7, and a separate 3x3 block with its center changed to 7. Another test was solved correctly by filling the 5x5 frame's 3x3 cavity 7 and replacing the missing center of a separate 3x3 color9 object with 7.

Expanded recurrence, additional current validated variant (one demo; test solved on third submission with two wrong attempts): background 3. Demo shows a 7x7 outline with interior 5x5 filled 7; a separate 3x3 outline with only center empty has its center changed to 7. Test contained (a) 4x4 outline color4 with 2x2 cavity -> fill 2; (b) 7x7 outline color1 with 5x5 cavity -> fill 7; (c) 3x3 color8 object missing center -> center becomes 7. These reinforce the cavity-size mapping: 2x2 ->2, 3x3/5x5 ->7, and isolated center hole in 3x3 ->7. Validate grid serialization strictly: prior first guess malformed due wrong row width; second structurally valid but wrong because it used 7 for 2x2 cavity. Correct output preserves all outlines/exterior and applies the corresponding interior fill.

Expanded recurrence, 3 demos, test solved after five wrong submissions:
- Demo 1: 10x10 bg4; 7x7 square frame of 6 at rows1–7, cols0–6, cavity rows2–6, cols1–5 -> 7. This is a 5x5 interior. Confirms the large framed cavity fill color 7.
- Demo 2: 30x18 bg8. Multiple objects: 7x7 frame of 9 at r2–8,c4–10, interior 5x5 ->7; 3x3 frame of 3 at r1–3,c13–15 with one missing center at r2,c14 ->7; 4x4 frame of 3 at r10–13,c11–14 with 2x2 interior r11–12,c12–13 ->2; 9x7 frame of 6 at r14–20,c2–8 with interior r15–19,c3–7 ->7; 3x3 frame of 1 at r16–18,c10–12 with missing center ->7; another 3x3 frame of 1 at r21–23,c10–12 center ->7; 3x3 frame of 9 at r26–28,c5–7 center ->7; 3x3 frame of 0 at r26–28,c10–12 center ->7. Note the 2x2 cavity specifically filled with 2; multiple frame/component types coexist.
- Demo 3: 15x22 bg8. 5x5 frame of 4 at r0–4,c0–4 interior 3x3 ->7; 4x4 frame of 3 at r1–4,c15–18, interior 2x2 ->2; 5x5 frame of 6 at r6–12,c5–9, interior 5x3 ->7; 6x6 frame of 9 at r7–12,c15–20, interior 4x4 ->2. Thus 3x3 or 5x3 cavities get 7; 2x2 and 4x4 cavities get 2, regardless of frame color. The 3x3 objects with only center empty are also filled 7.

Solved test input 15x20, background 3: a 5x5 frame of 5 at r3–7,c2–6 with 3x3 interior r4–6,c3–5 filled 7; a 3x3 object of 6 at r10–12,c3–5 with center (11,4) changed to 7; a 5x5 frame of 5 at r9–13,c10–14 with 3x3 interior r10–12,c11–13 filled 7; a 7x7 frame of 4 at r0–7,c8–15 with 5x5 interior r1–6,c9–14 filled 2. This last large cavity requires 2, not 7. Correct submission was reached on wrong attempt 6, after five failed guesses.

General inference strongly supported: cavity dimensions determine fill color, at least in observed shapes: 2x2 or 4x4 ->2; 3x3, 5x3, 5x5 ->7. A centered single-cell hole in a 3x3 object ->7. Preserve border and exterior. For future variants, request demos when cavity-size mapping uncertain; don't use one global color for all interiors. Verify exact frame bounds and cavity dimensions.
## task-55b70234: framed cavity fill colors (new demo evidence)

A fresh 11x21 test was solved after the first grid submission was structurally invalid, one demo, and a corrected submission. Demo (11x10, bg=0) shows three separate outlined objects:
- 4x4 color-3 frame at rows0-3, cols0-3; its 2x2 interior (r1-2,c1-2) is filled with 2.
- 4x4 color-6 frame at rows2-5, cols5-8; its 2x2 interior (r3-4,c6-7) is filled with 2.
- 3x3 color-1 frame at rows7-9, cols3-5; its 1x1 center (r8,c4) is filled with 7.
Thus for this instance, 2x2 square cavities receive 2; a single-cell center cavity in a 3x3 outline receives 7. Preserve frames and background/exterior.

Correct test transformation: preserve all four outlines. Fill the 2x2 interior of the 4x4 color-1 frame (rows1-2, cols9-10) with 2. Fill the 3x3 cavity of the 5x5 color-5 frame (rows5-7, cols15-17) with 7. Fill the 3x3 cavity of the 5x5 color-8 frame (rows6-8, cols6-8) with 7. The previously submitted first attempt was INVALID ARC GRID because one row had the wrong width, despite the intended fills; corrected output was accepted. Always machine-check every row length and total dimensions before submission.

## task-d795d9b6 recurrence: marker interval variant with explicit singleton negative evidence
A fresh variant had background 7 and marker 4. In its only demo, row 4 contained markers at columns 2, 3, and 9; output recolored columns 4–8 to 3, leaving the markers intact. This supports recoloring background cells strictly between consecutive markers on a row (there were no demonstrated vertical pairs). The test had background 2 and a single marker 4 at row 1, column 9; correct output is unchanged, since there is no consecutive marker pair. This was accepted. Do not assume singleton markers or simply uniform-looking lines should change. As with other task-d795d9b6 variants, ground from current demos; other recurrences have demonstrated additional row-and-column interval behavior or different rules.

### Newly validated variant (one demo): consecutive-marker interpolation on both axes
A fresh task-d795d9b6 instance had one demo with background 4 and marker 2; the output color was 3. Input-output deltas establish that, on each row and independently on each column, recolor only background cells strictly between consecutive marker cells to 3. Preserve all marker cells and all cells not inside such intervals; use marker positions from the original input. Demo checks: row 0 markers at c3, c6, c9, c13, c17 caused intervening background runs to become 3, while cells outside the first/last bracket stayed 4. Column 3 markers at r9 and r12 caused the intervening r10–11 cells to become 3. Other unbracketed cells remained unchanged. This rule correctly solved the test (bg7, marker5) with horizontal and vertical intervals processed from original marker coordinates. Confirm current demos because this task ID has other variants.

### Solved variant: row/column interpolation independently
чA fresh instance (bg=2, marker=6) had a single demo (bg=1, marker=4; output color=3). The demonstrated rule is to recolor to 3 only background cells strictly between consecutive marker cells in each row and independently in each column. Keep markers unchanged and leave unbracketed cells untouched; use marker coordinates from the original input rather than treating newly filled cells as markers. This explained demo horizontal segments and adjacent markers (no background between them), plus vertical interpolation. Correct test output included horizontal intervals in rows with multiple markers and vertical intervals in columns with multiple markers (e.g. same-column markers at r4/r8 filled r5-r7); accepted with no wrong submissions. This task ID has other variants, so confirm using current demos.

## task-d795d9b6 recurrence: between-marker intervals, demo-validated.

Eight demos established a variant where a uniform-background sparse-marker field is transformed by coloring only the background cells strictly between consecutive markers on each row or column. In the solved instance, bg=1, marker=2, output=3; preserve all markers and all unbracketed cells. Demos 5 and 8 directly show both horizontal and vertical intervals; e.g. demo5 row9 markers at c2 and c25 color c3–24, and demo8 c0 markers at r0 and r4 color r1–3. Snapshot marker locations from the input and process consecutive pairs only. Task ID d795d9b6 has other variants (including rays), so verify current demos.

### Additional solved recurrence variant (3 demos; test accepted)
A fresh task-d795d9b6 instance had sparse marker grids and three highly varied demos, showing the task ID alone does not identify the operation. Backgrounds/markers varied (demo1 bg=0, marker=5; demo2 bg=5, marker=0; demo3 bg=2, marker=6); in all cases output color was 3. Accepted test rule: on each row, recolor the background cells strictly between each pair of *consecutive* marker cells to 3; separately do the same on each column. Keep markers unchanged and preserve all cells not inside these intervals. Use original marker positions (do not let newly colored 3s become endpoints). Demo3 confirmed the rule even for adjacent markers: input row `[6,2,6,2,...]` became `[6,3,6,2,...]`, meaning the background cell between the first two markers became 3, while adjacent marker cells remain untouched. This rule correctly solved the test with bg=7, marker=8, output=3. Earlier incorrect first submission extended intervals across all marker endpoints/lines, coloring unsupported regions; correct approach is consecutive marker pairs only. For implementation: snapshot input; for each row, sort marker columns and fill open intervals between neighbors; then each column, sort marker rows and fill open intervals. Preserve endpoints and unrelated cells. This instance's test had 21x8; accepted output is derivable by that algorithm.

#### Demo2 caution / variant behavior
The second demo had larger bg=5/marker=0 grid and demonstrated substantial changed areas, apparently the same row/column intervals between neighboring markers. Analyze by *consecutive* marker pairs rather than treating every marker line or all spaces as fill. Some cells may appear as changed beyond a visually simple interpolation at first glance; map exact coordinates if another recurrence tests a similar version.

#### Critical lesson from recurrence
A previous skill note claimed eight demos were available; current actual instance proved a similar interpolation mechanism but at three demos, with a strongly atypical third demonstration of two adjacent markers. Do not require minimum marker counts; a pair is enough. D795d9b6 family can feature multiple variants, including rays or other patterns, and historical ID-linked notes are only hypotheses. Ground each new instance in its current demos and any selector evidence; request more if the task’s behavior is not explained by every observed pair.


## task-3f9edb0d: embedded-shape noise cleanup (validated)
One demo: grid background 6, with a uniform 4x4 block of 1s at rows2-5, cols4-7 and a uniform 7x7 block of 2s at rows2-6, cols12-18. Sparse anomalies (including other colors and background-color cells) within these rectangles were all normalized to the block's dominant fill (1 or 2); same-color flecks outside the two rectangles were removed/replaced by background 6. Thus the task extracts solid monochrome rectangles, suppresses scattered noise, and restores outside to background. Current test had background 8, 6x5 block color7 at r0-4,c4-9; 3x3 block color7 at r9-15,c10-12; 5x3 block color4 at r25-27,c8-12. All other non-8 speckles outside those blocks were converted to background 8; cells inside blocks normalized to their solid block colors. The output was accepted. Infer regions from coherent rectangular mass, but verify shapes and any adjacent noise from the current input/demo; dimensions need not match demo.

## Workflow
1. Treat every instance as fresh evidence. Prior task-family patterns can suggest hypotheses, but cannot establish the current rule.
2. Compare demo inputs and outputs cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, input/output values, and connected changed regions.
3. Identify candidate sources and targets only after mapping changes. Verify a transformation against multiple regions and demos.
4. Before applying the rule, state which observed changes it explains and which cells remain untouched.
5. If examples show a different geometry or operation from the expected pattern, discard that expectation. Request another demo when uncertainty remains and its cost beats speculation.

## task-d871171c: full-line recoloring to 2 (demo-validated)
A fresh instance demo established: recolor to 2 every complete line whose input cells are all the foreground marker color, preserving all other cells. Demo input 7x10 used background 5 and marker 8. Full vertical columns 3 and 6 (all 8s) were changed to 2, as was full horizontal row 3; partial lines/other cells remained unchanged. In the test, background 4, marker 3: the full bottom row of 3s and full columns 6 and 15 of 3s were recolored 2; partial rows/columns and all remaining cells were preserved. Important serialization pitfall: one submitted grid had row 0 width 21 instead of 22 and was rejected as invalid ARC grid; ensure each row length matches. The corrected exact 5x22 grid was accepted. Current demos establish eligible color by which lines are fully uniform, not assuming a fixed marker color. Check each row/column against original grid and recolor only complete uniform lines.

## Pitfalls
- Familiar colors or sparse markers do not imply a familiar operation; colors can play unrelated roles.
- Do not stop after one plausible local example. Check all changed regions and demos for alignment, preservation, and exceptions.
- Unchanged cells are not evidence of a transformed footprint; base analysis on actual input/output differences.

## Reference
See `references/demo-grounding-example.md` for why changed-cell mapping should precede pattern assumptions.

# Budget discipline for interactive ARC

Use for interactive ARC tasks where demos and wrong submissions consume a limited attempt budget and each turn must end in one action object.

## Procedure
1. Read the current evaluator state, budget, test grid, and any newly supplied demo pair.
2. Map demo input/output differences directly. Record affected coordinates, colors, preserved example components, and geometry linking edits to source objects.
3. Maintain only a few competing hypotheses. For each proposed demo request, identify in advance which hypotheses it could distinguish.
4. After receiving a demo, immediately make one substantive decision: request another only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses at acceptable cost; otherwise submit the best-supported output.
5. Do not spend turns on repeated tool calls, placeholder commands, or redundant independent analyses that do not change evidence or inference. Under strict evaluator protocols, use no unrelated tools during puzzle turns.
6. Keep every puzzle reply protocol-only and end with exactly one valid action JSON. Validate submitted dimensions, row widths, and values; preserve unsupported cells.

## Pitfalls
- More demos do not automatically reduce uncertainty; evaluate by expected discrimination.
- A single demo can show edits without identifying the rule selecting affected objects. Do not extrapolate a partial pattern across similar test objects.
- Tool activity is not progress: avoid repeated delegation or placeholder terminal calls, particularly where turns or runtime budgets are constrained.
- The required final action format is part of correctness; append no prose after the action object.
